## New research across more than 200 enterprises looks at how shared knowledge can help companies coordinate their agents—and turn lessons from their work into an operational edge.

At Microsoft, we talk with business leaders every day about how becoming a Frontier Firm means building a self-reinforcing system of learning across the organization. They understand the idea. What they want to know is how to put it to work: What does this look like in my company? What are the organizations furthest ahead actually doing? And how do I know we’re making progress?

To date, studies that point to actionable guidance on firm-wide transformation have been limited. New research Microsoft launched in collaboration with global technology and advisory firm Keystone measured where major enterprises are today and found patterns that suggest promising paths others can follow. 1

The net: many companies are already building agents and putting them to work. As agents take on more, the challenge is now how to orchestrate and learn from them. One way to meet that challenge is a knowledge spine : a shared system that stores and updates the context agents rely on, along with the corrections, tests, and lessons that come from the agents’ work. Among companies in the study, those with more of the practices the researchers measured in place—including the pieces of a knowledge spine—also saw bigger gains in operating margins and return on assets from 2022 to 2025. 2 What a company’s agents learn on the job is valuable intelligence that belongs to that company alone.

Only 3% of companies in the sample have deployed the building blocks for a knowledge spine—but they illuminate an approach that other organizations can follow. 3 That said, it’s early days, and this research shows correlation, not causation, which means there’s more work to be done and more to learn about the transformation journey we’re all on together.

## About the research

To see what practices set those companies apart, the research team first interviewed leaders at 29 organizations with advanced AI deployments, including 18 AI-native startups, to identify operational commonalities. 4 They then translated those findings into a detailed questionnaire and used it to assess more than 200 other enterprises, public and private. Every enterprise in the sample has more than 1,000 employees, and together they span sectors including financial services, manufacturing, healthcare, retail, and technology. All the companies were already using AI, so the sample doesn’t represent the economy as a whole. 5 The questionnaire scored each company on the practices it has in place to build, run, coordinate, check, and learn from its agents.

## A framework for transformation

To provide a framework for understanding enterprise transformation, the researchers grouped the companies into four stages based on their scores on the questionnaire. 6 Those in stage one exhibit a patchwork of AI pilot projects and often don’t have AI deployments beyond chat. The efforts lack coordination, are not connected to real business workflows, and seem to show minimal business impact.

At stage two, companies use agents to tackle real business. They target specific workflows across a variety of functions but lack systems for management and orchestration. Instead, they create teams and committees to prioritize AI investments, provide checks and balances, and manage scattered efforts. In essence, humans coordinate agents and check their work. Not surprisingly, human orchestration is hard to scale, which can make returns more difficult to realize.

Stage three is the turning point. Companies start using systems, not people, to coordinate agents—some by sharing a common knowledge base, others by closely monitoring agent work—with business outcomes guiding which work agents take on. Researchers heard from some companies that this mostly happens in parts of the business, such as one department or a few workflows, which is a practical place to start.

At stage four, these practices come together. Most have orchestration, governance, and a knowledge spine in place, and many feed lessons from agents’ work back into the shared knowledge and tests they rely on. 7 That’s the direction of travel: a single agentic operating model, where systems take on more of the coordination and learning.

Four stages of enterprise transformation

Companies in the study were grouped into four stages of AI maturity. Stage three marks the start of a key breakthrough: shifting coordination of work from people to systems.

## Where the returns show up

The team compared financial results from 2022 to 2025 for more than 100 public companies in the study, looking at how companies in the top two quartiles of questionnaire scores fared against those in the bottom quartiles. Companies that scored in the top quartile improved operating margins by over 5 percentage points more than those in the bottom quartile and return on assets by about 2 percentage points more. 8 Put simply, the higher a company scored, the more its margins tended to grow. These financial results cover a span of time that precedes most of today’s agent systems. So the study can’t say agents drove those margins, only that the highest-scoring companies were already doing something right. Additional research is planned to test cause and effect.

Why did margins barely move for companies in the bottom two quartiles? The researchers point to an idea economists call the J-curve: when a major new technology arrives, the payoff can dip or lag while companies reorganize work around it, then climb once those changes take hold. 9 With agents, the lag may come from deploying them faster than building the systems to coordinate them. Still, if the payoff can lag, how a company manages AI spending along the way matters.
